content.title: Response to Reviewer PzAV
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments and suggestions.. We've included responses and additional results below. 

**1: LGA could escape local optimums.** Except for the theoretical analysis for the convex function, we also analyze LGA under the convergence proof of Adam in appendix A.2. The analysis under Adam also shows LGA can meet the convergence requirements of the optimization algorithm. And the reason why LGA could escape local optimums is also shown in the conclusion of appendix A.2. As for the convergence rate, we have removed it in the rebuttal revision. Experimentally, we practice our method in MNIST and CIFAR-10 on the task of autoencoder, which is a standard problem for evaluating optimization methods on neural networks. The result shown in Table 12 in the rebuttal revision indicate that our method is useful to help gradient-based optimizers to "jump" some local minima.

**2: Experiment settings.** Our work focus on the performance of LGA under the same experimental setting, which does not conflict with the experimental result and analysis. The training strategy with different learning rate schedulers has been conducted, and the experimental result is shown in Table 5. Besides, in the image segmentation task, the AutoEval task, the video sentence grounding task, and the autoencoder task (appendix A.5~A.8), we use the same settings with the cited works without further tuning. Those results also show that our approach is effective and stable for different optimization algorithm.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a loss-aware gradient adjusting strategy (LGA) based on the loss status. LGA utilizes the loss-incentive correction term to adjusts the magnitude of gradients. The key step is to estimate an“oracle”lower bound of the objective value. Then LGA can estimate the distance between the current position and the optimal solution. Experiments on standard datasets test the effectiveness of the proposed approach by incorporating into various gradient-based methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength：
The paper presents an alternative approach to neural network optimization by exploring the status of the loss. The proposed strategy can be applied to various gradient descent-based methods. The paper also proofs the convergence for convex problems. Extensive experiments demonstrate the advantages.  

Weaknesses: 
It is claimed that the proposed loss-incentive correction term provides extra energy to jump out of some local optimal solutions. However, the claim is not well-supported by the experiments. The detail comments are as follows.
1.	Subsection 3.3 is very important. It discusses the mechanism of the loss-incentive term. However, it is not so clear. At the beginning of the training, the loss f_{x_t} is decreasing with an appropriate learning rate. So the estimation of the lower bound of f_x in (3) is always smaller than f_{x_t}. So \Omega(f_{x_t}) in (4) is always equal to 0. Then how the proposed approach jumps out of the local optimal solution? It needs to explain this issue in more detail. Also, why use the moving average in (3)? Overall, the estimation of the oracle lower bound of f_x needs more elaborations.
2.	It is better test with loss function having known local and global optimal solutions. Also, training autoencoders on benchmark datasets is considered as a standard problem for evaluating optimization methods on neural networks. It is especially for evaluating the escape from local optimal solutions. For the three deep autoencoders in the following paper. 
G. E. Hinton and R. R. Salakhutdinov, “Reducing the dimensionality of data with neural networks,” Science, vol. 313, no. 5786, pp. 504–507, 2006.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ther
content.comment:
Thank you for your careful reading and the constructive feedback. We've included responses and additional results below. 

**1: Subsection 3.3.** We have revised subsection 3.3 in the rebuttal revision, adding the explanation of the components of the loss-incentive term and the associated design motivations. 

**2: The estimation of the lower bound.** At the beginning of the training, the estimation of the lower bound of f_x in (3) is always smaller than f_{x_t}. So \Omega(f_{x_t}) in (4) is always bigger than 0, which makes the loss-incentive correction term work and provides extra energy for parameters to jump out of some local optimum solutions.

**3: Why use the moving average in Eq.(3).** The reason is that the loss function will gradually converge to the target loss status with increasing epoch, so the larger the epoch, the higher the reference value of the loss function for the estimation of the target loss. And we compare the moving average in Eq.(3) to two variants, the comparison result shown in Table 13 indicates the moving average is better. 

**4: Training Autoencoder.** Thank you for the suggestion. We present the results of the training autoencoder on MNIST and CIFAR-10 in Table 12 in the rebuttal revision. The contrastive result support that the proposed strategy is useful to help gradient-based optimizers to escape from some local optimal solutions.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
1. Empirically the proposed method seems to perform well on standard vision and NLP tasks

Cons:
1. One of my major concerns of the paper in its current form is that it offers very little motivation behind why the proposed approach works. Specifically, the term "loss status" isn't clearly defined. The loss-incentive term and their components \Omega and \varphi have very little basis and the paper offers very little intuition as to why the term should help. I strongly recommend the authors to provide more insights on the above via more experiments and/or additional theoretical analysis.

2. The convergence analysis is weak and offers no new insight on why the update works. The update supposedly helps gradient based optimizers to "jump" local minima, but the analysis (in the realizability setting) is for strongly convex functions. The main convergence result in itself done on just one dimension. 

3. The related works section is also very sparse and can be greatly improved. Some of the cited works in the convergence efficiency paragraph aren't relevant to the current work.

4. The experiment section can benefit greatly from improved analysis. The justification of why the proposed algorithm works better isn't convincing. This is the place where one could empirically justify the choice of \Omega and \varphi and additionally show experiments on other choices of \Omega and \varphi, given that they aren't based on any guiding principles.

content.title: Response to Reviewer EJ71
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments and suggestions. We've included responses and additional results below.

**1: Motivation.** The core idea of LGA is that adding incentive gives the model more chances to escape and find a new local minimum, rather than be trapped in a local minimum or flattened area. And the loss function is a direct reflection of the training state, which can indicate the overall progress of the optimization. Besides, we have revised subsection 3.1 and 3.3 in the rebuttal revision, adding the explanation of the design of the components of the loss-incentive term and the associated design motivations. 

**2: The theoretical analysis.** Besides the theoretical analysis only for the convex function, we also analyze LGA under the convergence proof of Adam in appendix A.2. The analysis under Adam also shows LGA will not affect the convergence of the original algorithm. The convergence result on just one dimension has been revised to d dimension.

**3: Related works.** We have revised the related works section in the rebuttal revision.

**4: Additional results.** To verify the proposed lower bound estimation, we compare our method to two common estimation operations, averaging all the loss statuses and summing up the loss status with momentum strategy, in MNIST and CIFAR-10. The result shown in Table.13 in the rebuttal revision support our design is more reasonable.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The author proposed a new method named loss-aware gradient adjusting strategy (LGA) to help the deep neural network avoid bad local minimum points. LGA combines the loss information and gradient information to modify the gradient of parameters. It adjusts the updated magnitude of parameters. And LGA can be applied into different DNN optimizers.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
1. The motivation for the work is clear.
2. It provides a new method to help DNNs to find good local minima.
3. No much additional computation gain is used for the proposed methods. 

Weaknesses
1. The proposed method is too trivial. There are too many hyper-parameters in the proposed LGA to be tuned.
2. The theoretical analysis on regret bound is only for the convex function with too strong assumptions, which 
    usually does not holds for training DNNs.
3. The experiments are not convincing. I can believe the baseline of CIFAR-100 is only about 30% accuracy used in the paper. 
    In my experience, the baseline of CIFAR-100 should be more than 75% accuracy.
4. No large-scale dataset is used to evaluate the proposed method.
5. Some figures, e.g., Figure 2, are not clear. Please give the title and legend for each subfigure.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer Aymh
content.comment:
Thank you for the constructive feedback. We've included responses and additional results below. 

**1: Too many hyper-parameters**. LGA involves 3 hyperparameters, \gamma_2, \varepsilon and \xi. Only \gamma_2 needs to be tuned.  . After giving the initial value of  \gamma_2, LGA will adaptively modify it according to the changes in the loss status.  And the setting of \varepsilon can be regarded as a truncation mechanism, which can stop LGA when it has little influence for parameter updates. \xi is used to keep the denominator of the loss-incentive correction term in a non-zero state. Therefore, \varepsilon and \xi are easy to set and don't need to be tuned.

**2: The theoretical analysis**. Besides the theoretical analysis for the convex function in appendix A.1, we also analyze LGA under the convergence proof of Adam in appendix A.2. The analysis under Adam also shows LGA can meet the convergence requirements of the optimization algorithm.

**3: The baseline of CIFAR-100**. In this work, we mainly focus on the performance of LGA under the same experimental setting, which does not conflict with the experimental result of CIFAR100. Besides, in the image segmentation task, the AutoEval task, the video sentence grounding task, and the autoencoder task (appendix A.5~A.8), we use the same settings with the cited works without further tuning. 

**4: The problem of Figure 2**. Thanks for the suggestion. We have given the title and legend for each subfigure in Figure 2 in the rebuttal revision.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
This work proposes an optimizer where the gradient is adjusted in a "loss-aware" manner. The paper includes analysis on the convergence rate as well as empirical evaluations on various datasets.

There are quite a few weaknesses unfortunately in the paper that are shared by many reviewers (and myself):

+ Unconvincing experiments, particularly with a CIFAR-100 baseline that only achieves 30% accuracy
+ Convergence analysis is rather weak and makes very strong assumptions
+ The main claim is that the proposed technique can escape local optimum, but it's not really vaildated

All reviewers leaned toward reject, and I agree with their opinion.
